newsitem.title: USA: DC CFO says says next 12 mos "critical" for city.
newsitem.headline: DC CFO says says next 12 mos "critical" for city.

text.p: With a new fiscal year dawning next week for the financially embattled District of Columbia, city officials are gearing up for a tough and pivotal year, D.C.'s chief financial officer said.

"The next 12 months will be critical in terms of ... the District's ability to lift itself from the current financial crisis," Anthony Williams told the city's financial control board at a hearing on the D.C.'s readiness to implement a $5.02 billion fiscal year 1997 budget.

"It (soon) wil become obvious whether the District government has the conviction and the descipline to sustain the long journey back to fiscal stability," Williams told the board, headed by economist Andrew Brimmer.
Brimmer noted the FY'97 budget will be the first 12-month budget to be implemented by the District under the watchful eye of the control board, created in April 1995.
He said the city's success hinges on its ability to do more than $140 million in savings and cost reductions set for FY'97.

Williams said after months of "emergency actions to combat the effect of years of financial mismanagement and neglect," the city now has some "breathing room" to take a longer-term look at its financial operation.
He said the city will seek proposals for a new financial management system by November 1 and expects the system's first "module" to operate by October 1.
Williams said it will be more difficult for D.C. to meet its budget target for FY'97 that it was for FY'96.

"We have a mixed outlook for FY'97," Williams said. "We are in far better position to implement the FY'97 budget that we were for FY'96, but then, the challenge is much greater this time around," Williams said.
He said his office will monitor the financial performance of city agencies on a weekly and monthly basis.
Williams added D.C. will not be able to meet its 1997 budget target without major changes in the procurement prcoess."
Currently, Williams said, most D.C. agencies still enter into contracts without having the CFO certify that funds are available.
And most agencies still award contracts noncompetitively, which means they paying far too much for supplies and services, Williams said.
"We need immediate action" to deal with these problems, he said.
